qs.q: A young male patient experiences recurrent joint bleeds and easy bruising. Coagulation screening reveals a normal prothrombin time, prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time, and normal thrombin time. This pattern points to a deficiency in which pathway?
qs.e: A normal prothrombin time combined with a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time points specifically to an intrinsic pathway factor deficiency such as Haemophilia A or B. Extrinsic pathway defects would cause an isolated prolongation of the prothrombin time.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following conditions or substances is known to cause a prolonged thrombin time?
qs.e: Thrombin time measures the rate of fibrinogen conversion to fibrin and is prolonged by hypofibrinogenemia, heparin, elevated FDPs, and dysfibrinogenemia. Factor XII deficiency does not cause bleeding or alter the thrombin time.

qs.q: A 20-year-old man presents with recurrent joint bleeds. His prothrombin time is normal, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is prolonged, thrombin time (TT) is normal. Which coagulation factor abnormality is most likely?
o: Congenital deficiency of plasma Factor VII
Acquired deficiency of systemic Vitamin K
Congenital deficiency of plasma Factor VIII
qs.e: An isolated prolonged APTT with normal PT and TT, plus haemarthroses, is classic for haemophilia A.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Thrombin time (TT) measures the final step of clot formation: conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin. It helps identify fibrinogen deficiencies or the presence of thrombin inhibitors such as heparin.

sections.p: Thrombin time is a laboratory assay that adds excess thrombin to plasma and records the time for a clot to appear. Normal range is roughly 10–14 seconds.
b: Reflects fibrinogen quantity and function
Detects direct thrombin inhibition

t.b: Does the patient have adequate functional fibrinogen or a thrombin inhibitor? Prolonged TT suggests low fibrinogen, dysfibrinogenemia, or heparin effect; normal TT excludes these.

sections.p: There is no formal staging; severity is inferred from TT length and associated clinical bleeding.
b: Mild: TT 15–20 s, minor bleeding
Moderate: TT 20–30 s, mucosal bleeding
Severe: TT >30 s, spontaneous hemorrhage

sections.p: Identify whether the problem lies in fibrinogen quantity, quality, or thrombin inhibition.
b: Fibrinogen deficiency (congenital or consumptive, e.g., massive bleeding, DIC)
Dysfibrinogenemia (genetic or acquired, e.g., liver disease, snake venom)
Heparin therapy or heparin contamination
Direct thrombin inhibitors (e.g., dabigatran, argatroban)
Rare inhibitors (e.g., lupus anticoagulant interfering with assay)

sections.p: Patients may have mucosal bleeding, easy bruising, or prolonged bleeding after surgery. In low‑resource settings, severe fibrinogen loss can follow trauma, obstetric hemorrhage, or severe malaria.
b: Bleeding from gums, nose, or IV sites
Excessive surgical or postpartum hemorrhage

sections.p: Combine TT with other coagulation tests to locate the defect.

t.b: Is the extrinsic pathway abnormal? Normal PT with prolonged TT points to fibrinogen or thrombin inhibition.
Is the intrinsic pathway abnormal? Prolonged aPTT with normal TT suggests factor deficiencies, not fibrinogen problems.
What is the quantitative fibrinogen level? Low level confirms deficiency; normal level with prolonged TT suggests dysfibrinogenemia or inhibitor.
Is heparin causing the prolongation? Reversal normalizes TT, confirming heparin effect.
Does adding normal plasma correct TT? Correction indicates deficiency; lack of correction suggests inhibitor.

sections.p: Severe fibrinogen deficiency can precipitate uncontrolled hemorrhage, especially in trauma, obstetrics, or surgery.
b: Rapidly falling fibrinogen in DIC
Massive postpartum hemorrhage
Uncontrolled bleeding after major surgery

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then replace fibrinogen or neutralize inhibitors.
b: Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate for deficiency or dysfibrinogenemia
Stop heparin or direct thrombin inhibitor; give protamine (heparin) or idarucizumab (dabigatran) if needed
Supportive care: maintain blood pressure, replace lost blood, monitor labs

sections.p: Re‑check TT and fibrinogen after therapy. In chronic conditions, monitor periodically and educate patients on bleeding risk.
b: Repeat TT 6–12 h after replacement
Screen for liver disease or ongoing consumption in DIC

sections.p: Other clotting assays that assess earlier steps of the cascade.
b: Prothrombin Time (PT) – evaluates extrinsic pathway, not fibrinogen conversion
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) – evaluates intrinsic pathway
Bleeding time – assesses platelet function, not coagulation

sections.p: Certain conditions may give a normal TT despite a problem, or a prolonged TT unrelated to fibrinogen.
b: High heparin levels can be neutralized by excess thrombin, giving a falsely normal TT
Low plasma fibrinogen with high levels of fibrin degradation products may yield borderline TT
Laboratory error: improper sample handling can artificially prolong TT

whenToSeekHelp: Uncontrolled bleeding after trauma or surgery

faq.q: Why is TT normal when PT and aPTT are abnormal?
faq.a: Because TT tests only the final step; PT/aPTT abnormalities usually reflect factor deficiencies, not fibrinogen or thrombin inhibition.
Yes; heparin prolongs TT, and the effect disappears after protamine neutralization.

faq.q: What is the difference between fibrinogen deficiency and dysfibrinogenemia?
faq.a: Deficiency means low quantity; dysfibrinogenemia means normal quantity but abnormal function, both can prolong TT.

exam: Explain how thrombin time helps differentiate between a fibrinogen deficiency and a heparin effect.
